children.author: h4x3rotab
children.text:
Cofounder of Phala here. Happy to explain it.

The TEEs are real. The problem was caused by software bugs. Running a TEE app (CVM) is more than dropping a binary into TEE. Two problems remain: (1) migration, you don’t want to completely lose the data if the hardware dies, and (2) upgradability, you want to patch the app when there’s a bug without building the state from scratch. So we want to decouple the states from hardware.

Using the hardware key is painful. The solution is to introduce a separate key manager (KMS). It releases keys to the app iff. the app follows a predefined “policy” (code, hardware attestation, etc). We can decouple the states from hardware based on a remote KMS.

This is rather a common design. You can find it in our system, as well as other mature frameworks like Confidential Containers.

As the system grows, a bug was introduced to the policy of how we replicate a KMS’s key material (for redundancy). The attacker exploited it with multiple sophisticated attacks, eventually being able to cheat a running KMS to hand over the keys to a fake one, like it’s a legit KMS replica. As a result, the keys protected by the KMS became at risk.

To mitigate the problem, the legacy KMS was dropped and a new KMS was deployed. We have then rotated all the keys associated with the legacy KMS. A series of protocol and code audit is ongoing to prevent future failure.

> having their "software TEE" root keys hacked

Did they? It says the attacker was able to create unauthorized CVMs (makes sense), able to obtain application credentials (significance unclear to me), and that they rotated their KMS root key in response (which is confusing to me because if they use hardware backed keys then I don't understand how the root key could ever be compromised).

So does this imply they aren't actually providing a proper hardware backed TEE? But that's also confusing because at least if you provision a VM you can have the hardware attest to its state.

This revealed something as delightful as a purported TEE provider having their "software TEE" root keys hacked, through "a legacy internet-facing service with management interfaces that relied on loopback access for trust and did not independently authenticate callers" (https://phala.com/posts/phala-november-preliminary-incident-...)

Decision models can be cheap because it’s a fundamentally cheaper technology than LLMs. So that part isn’t suspicious at all to me.

That said, if you don’t believe OpenAI when they say they don’t train on your decision API inputs you shouldn’t trust them regarding LLM inputs either.

As an aside, I always wondered about decision models. They are so cheap. I can’t help but think that providers must be using them as honeypots for data acquisition:

You do dont find real world company documents on the web that you could train on. And companies certainly won’t upload them to you so you can improve your models, not even with incentives. But provide a model with dirt cheap input pricing and free outputs - and you gut yourself a firehose.

To think that the “labs” wouldn’t train on this is like thinking they’d never have trained on shadow library books because, “well, it’s illegal”. They did it back then and it gave them an advantage over the competition. So why wouldn’t they now?
